newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Martin beats deficit target, sets new one.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Martin beats deficit target, sets new one.

text.p: Canadian Finance Minister Paul Martin said on Wednesday that Canada's 1995/96 budget deficit came in C$4.1 billion ($3 billion) lower than he originally projected and pledged to lower it to 1 percent of gross domestic product by 1998/99.
Martin, who delivered his autumn budget update to a parliamentary finance committee, added he was on target to meet his deficit projections for fiscal 1996/97 (April-March) and 1997-98.
He added that "we are very clearly on a track to a balanced budget," although he declined to specify when.
But despite recent pressure from politicians and businesses, Martin said he would offer no tax cuts at this time.

"Those who would suggest we now alter course -- by bringing in a broad-based tax cut -- are wrong. Make no mistake. Offering a broad-based tax cut is certainly tempting," Martin said in a prepared speech.
"But should the government consider a broad-based tax cut when the fiscal challenge is not fully met? No. That would be simply irresponsible."
He said the final deficit for fiscal 1995/96 was C$28.6 billion ($20.9 billion), well below the C$32.7 billion ($23.9 billion) he forecast in last March's budget.

Martin said he was well on track to meet the 1996/97 deficit target of C$24.3 billion ($17.7 billion) or 3 percent of GDP. His 1997/98 deficit target of C$17 billion ($12.4 billion) or 2 percent of GDP was also within reach, Martin said.

Following his tradition of setting a series of two-year rolling targets for deficit reduction, Martin said on Wednesday he would reduce the deficit to C$9.0 billion ($6.6 billion) or 1 percent of GDP in 1998/99.
In the same year, Canada's financial requirement will drop to zero, meaning the country would not have to borrow new money in financial markets other than to roll over existing debt.

Martin also revised his economic growth forecasts, pegging GDP for 1996 at 1.5 percent, down from the 1.6 percent he projected in his March budget. He estimated growth in 1997 at 3 percent, above the 2.6 percent he forecast in his budget.
